name: Sarcee
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sapir, Edward. 1925. Pitch accent in Sarcee, an Athabaskan language. Journal de la Société des Américanistes de Paris, nouvelle série 17: 185-205.
catalog_locator: pp. 191 (last paragraph) - 192 (top), immediately before the section 'Tone' (pp. 192-193);extract pp. 7-8
catalog_quote: In pronouncing Sarcee, or any Athabaskan language, it is important to give each syllable its due weight. The syllable as such has a more clear-cut phonetic distinctness and a more individual morphological significance than the syllable of English or French, even if it is not always possible to assign it a concrete meaning. The syllables of a word do not generally differ greatly in stress, though the stress is of course not uniform. Certain elements, like third person plural gi- "they" and the radical syllable of the verb, are more strongly stressed than others (e. g. in k'ágits'a' "they cease to cry", gi- and the stem -ts'a' are more strongly stressed than k'a- "off" > "to cease", which, however, must not be slurred over). Variations of stress do not seem to be coordinated with differences of tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Sarsi (sars1236) is not in the catalog. The two works with stress in the title are one work: Sapir 1925 'Pitch accent in Sarcee' (Glottolog 677549 is a duplicate record with the Collected Works editor Golla listed as author). The open 1925 original (IA scan of JSA vol. 17, already held by the project from the morning pass) was read and the stress passage verified against the page scan (pp. 191-192): word stress is nearly even across syllables, the verb stem and some prefixes (3pl gi-) are more strongly stressed, no positional rule, and stress is independent of tone; the paper's main content is the three-level tone system. Reprint DOI 10.1515/9783110851090.169 (De Gruyter, pp. 169-190) is paywalled; Persée confirmed to lack JSA t.17/1925. Nothing else in the item list; unread candidates that might refine (not in the list of works with stress in the title): Cook 1984 A Sarcee Grammar (lending-only), Cook 1971 'Vowels and tones in Sarcee' Language 47 (DOI 10.2307/412193, JSTOR).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sarcee is a tone (pitch accent) language with high, middle and low tones (Sapir's section 'Tone', pp. 192ff.). Stress is weak and non-uniform: syllables of a word differ little in prominence; the verb stem (radical) syllable and certain morphemes such as 3pl gi- are somewhat more strongly stressed than other prefix syllables. Stress is thus morphologically anchored (root/stem prominence), not positional, and is independent of tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; Sapir only says stress is 'not uniform' and names the elements that carry relatively greater stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the note that weakly stressed prefixes like k'a- 'must not be slurred over'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (the syllables 'of a word'); examples are verb forms in citation; morphological prominence (verb stem, 3pl prefix), with tone described separately as the primary suprasegmental.
new_statements.identity_note: Sapir 1925 describes the Sarcee of the Sarcee Reserve near Calgary, Alberta, from 1922 fieldwork; this is the same single variety now called Tsuut'ina (sars1236, ISO srs). No dialect distinction is at issue. The 1996 Nanagusja guide uses the name Tsuut'ina for the same language.

new_statements.reading: Sarcee is a tone (pitch accent) language; word stress is weak and nearly level across syllables, with somewhat greater prominence on the verb stem (radical syllable) and on certain prefixes (e.g. 3pl gi-). No fixed positional stress (initial/penult/final) is stated, and stress is not a function of tone. For catalog purposes: tone language, no fixed word-stress position; prominence morphologically (stem) governed. Sapir's own first-hand fieldwork (summer 1922), the earliest and still the only explicit first-hand statement on Sarcee stress that this search of works with stress in the title could read; Cook 1984 A Sarcee Grammar (lending-only) and Cook 1971 Language 47 (JSTOR) remain unread and could refine it.

tone_statements.citation: McDonough, Joyce, Jared O'Loughlin & Christopher Cox. 2013. An investigation of the three tone system in Tsuut'ina (Dene). Proceedings of Meetings on Acoustics (ICA 2013 Montreal; 165th ASA meeting), paper 060219. Acoustical Society of America. DOI 10.1121/1.4800661. tone_statements.quote: Tsuut’ina is a tone language. Contrary to Dene tonogenesis theory and unlike reports on all other Dene tone languages, Tsuut’ina is reported to have three tones, H, L, M. [...] In this study we investigate the tonal distribution, realization patterns and tonal alignment in data collected from two fluent speakers reciting prepared wordlists and short discourses. Preliminary investigation indicates that, as reported, three tonal patterns emerge, M tone associated most often with a falling tone, with distinct distribution patterns arguably related to morphological factors. Furthermore M tone is more highly variable.

tone_statements.summary: 3 tones H, M, L (M phonetically mostly falling and more variable); acoustic confirmation of three tonal patterns; distribution partly morphological (stem vs prefix domains).
